concepts.def: The smallest unit of life; carries out the functions needed to live.
A cell with a nucleus enclosed in a membrane; e.g. animal, plant, fungus cells.
A smaller cell with no nucleus; DNA is a loop in the cytoplasm; e.g. bacteria.
Parts inside a cell with specific jobs: nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, chloroplasts.
Cells adapted for a specific role, e.g. red blood cell, sperm, root hair.
Undifferentiated cell that can divide to form many cell types.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Nutrition & Health — a core area of GCSE Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Nutrition & Health brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Nutrition & Health.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a prokaryote?
options: Human skin cell
Yeast
Bacterium
Onion cell
protein synthesis
photosynthesis
aerobic respiration
cell division

mcqs.q: What is the key difference between mitosis and meiosis?
options: Mitosis happens in plants and meiosis happens in animals.
Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid cells; meiosis produces four genetically different haploid cells (gametes).
A dominant allele physically destroys the recessive allele in the genome.
Mitosis and meiosis both produce gametes; they are basically the same.

mcqs.q: Why is the secondary immune response to a pathogen faster and stronger than the primary?
options: Mitosis happens in plants and meiosis happens in animals.
Memory cells generated during the primary response can rapidly proliferate and produce large amounts of specific antibody on re-exposure.
The pathogen becomes weaker after the primary exposure, so the body has an easier job.
The body produces a different, more powerful antibody during the secondary response.

mcqs.q: What does it mean for an allele to be 'dominant'?
options: A dominant allele is the most common allele in a population.
The body produces a different, more powerful antibody during the secondary response.
It is expressed in the phenotype when at least one copy is present (in a heterozygote).
A dominant allele physically destroys the recessive allele in the genome.

mcqs.q: A bacterium is 2 µm long. How many fit end-to-end across a 1 mm gap?
options: 750 bacteria
500 bacteria
250 bacteria
400 bacteria

mcqs.q: A diet is very low in vitamin C over several months. Which deficiency disease is most likely?
options: Scurvy
Anaemia
Rickets
Goitre

mcqs.q: A student tests a food for protein using the biuret test. A positive result is shown by the solution turning:
options: Purple
Brick-red
Blue-black
Colourless

mcqs.q: Why is fibre (roughage) important in a balanced diet even though it is not digested?
options: It helps the gut move food along and prevents constipation.
It is the main source of energy.
It is broken down into glucose for respiration.
It is needed to build new proteins.

mcqs.q: Bile helps the digestion of fats. Which statement best describes its role?
options: It emulsifies fat into small droplets, increasing surface area.
It is an enzyme that breaks fat into glucose.
It makes the small intestine more acidic.
It absorbs fat into the blood directly.
